title: Hide Artifacts: VBA Stomping
summary: VBA Stomping hides a malicious macro by removing or replacing the macro source code stored inside an Office document while leaving the compiled version that Office actually executes. Macro source lives in module streams, and each module stream carries a PerformanceCache holding compiled p-code. A separate project stream records which Office build the macro project targets. When the host build matches, Office runs the stored p-code and never reads the source text. Tools that scan only source text therefore see benign or even empty macros. Detection requires comparing source against compiled code, looking for blank or mismatched module streams, and treating macro-enabled documents that execute with no readable macro content as suspicious.

beginner.definition: Macros are small programs that can run inside Microsoft Office documents. They are written in a language called Visual Basic for Applications, or VBA. Office stores both the readable macro text and a compiled copy. VBA stomping replaces the readable text with harmless words while the compiled, harmful copy stays behind.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many security tools check only the readable macro text. If that text looks harmless, the tool reports that the document is safe. The harmful compiled copy can still run when the document opens. This lets an attacker slip past common malware checks. Analysts must therefore inspect both copies and not just one of them.
howItWorks: An Office document with macros stores the macro text in pieces called module streams.
Next to each module stream there is a cached compiled version, known as p-code.
Another stream records which Office version the macro project was built for.
The attacker replaces the readable macro text with harmless text or empty bytes.
When Office opens the file, it compares its own version with the recorded version.
If the two versions match, Office runs the cached compiled code and ignores the harmless text.
beginner.example: Imagine a takeaway shop that shows a printed menu on the counter. A food inspector reads the menu and sees only salad and soup, so the shop passes the check. Behind the counter there is a fridge full of meals cooked earlier from a different recipe. When a regular customer orders, the staff heat up the old meal instead of following the printed menu. VBA stomping works in that way. The visible recipe is harmless, but the pre-cooked harmful version is what actually runs.
takeaways: Macro documents carry both readable text and a compiled copy of the code.
Checking only one of those copies can miss a malicious macro.
A document that runs code while showing no macro text deserves investigation.

objectives: Explain what a macro is and why Office stores a compiled copy of macro code.
Describe how VBA stomping hides malicious code from source code scanners.
Explain the role of the project version stream in deciding what Office executes.
Identify analysis steps that compare macro source text with compiled code.
Recognise a document that executes code despite having no readable macro text.
